title: The abelian category of coefficient towers
statement:
Let $E/\Ql$ be finite and $T$ a scheme.

1. $\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E)$ is the category of
   $\mathcal O_{E,T}/\ell^\bullet$-modules in the topos of inverse systems
   (functors $\mathbf N_{\geq1}^{\mathrm{op}}\to$ sheaves) on $T_{\mathrm{proét}}$
   (compare Bhatt–Scholze, Section 3.5). It is a Grothendieck abelian category
   in which kernels, cokernels and filtered colimits are computed level by
   level; we use its ordinary derived category $D(\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E))$.
2. Evaluation at level $n$, $C_\bullet\mapsto C_n$, is an exact functor
   $\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E)\to\Mod(T_{\mathrm{proét}},\mathcal O_{E,T}/\ell^n)$; for
   $C_\bullet\in D(\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E))$ we write $C_n$ for its image
   in $D(T_{\mathrm{proét}},\mathcal O_E/\ell^n)$.
3. The transition maps induce, for $m\leq n$, *reduction maps*
   $$
   C_n\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,T}/\ell^n}\mathcal O_{E,T}/\ell^m\longrightarrow C_m
   \quad\text{in }D(T_{\mathrm{proét}},\mathcal O_E/\ell^m),
   $$
   natural in $C_\bullet$ and compatible with composition $m'\leq m\leq n$.

Let $E/\Ql$ be finite and $T$ a scheme. 1. $\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E)$ is the category of $\mathcal O_{E,T}/\ell^\bullet$-modules in the topos of inverse systems (functors $\mathbf N_{\geq1}^{\mathrm{op}}\to$ sheaves) on $T_{\mathrm{proét}}$ (compare Bhatt–Scholze, Section 3.5).

proof.text: Put $R_n=(\mathcal O_E/\ell^n)_T$ with the quotient maps $q_{n,m}:R_n\to R_m$ for $n\geq m\geq1$, and let $J=\mathbf N_{\geq1}^{\mathrm{op}}$. These are exactly the coefficient sheaves and transition conventions of [sk-def-sp-coefficient-towers]. Take the small pro-étale site $\mathcal C$ in the universes of [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site]. Apply the sheaf equivalence of [lem-weil-pbc-diagram-site-realization] to $J$: the site $\mathcal D=J^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C$ has coverings generated by coverings in $\mathcal C$ at a fixed index, and $\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}(J,\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C))$. The presheaf $R(n,U)=R_n(U)$, with restriction in $U$ and quotient maps in $n$, is a commutative ring sheaf, since each $R_n$ is one. A sheaf of $R$-modules on $\mathcal D$ is precisely a family of sheaves $M_n$ of $R_n$-modules with semilinear transitions: the condition that the module action commute with the arrow from level $n$ to level $m$ is $t_{n,m}(a x)=q_{n,m}(a)t_{n,m}(x)$. Module morphisms are precisely levelwise linear maps commuting with these transitions. This gives inverse additive equivalences $\operatorname{Mod}(R)\simeq\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E)$ and proves the ring-object description in (1). Here the cited diagram-site lemma supplies the underlying sheaf equivalence, not a claim that a varying ring diagram is constant; the module identification follows directly from [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. The abelian-axioms subtheorem uses the generalized vertical topology and its sheaf criterion from [lem-weil-pbc-diagram-site-topology] directly on ℕ × T.ProEt. The actual varying coefficient presheaf is a sheaf because each vertical slice is its recorded coefficient ring sheaf. Sending a full-subcategory object to the same presheaf with this sheaf proof, and back, gives inverse equivalences with the category of module sheaves; all morphisms are unchanged.

proof.text: Both $J$ and $\mathcal C$ are small in the chosen module universe, hence so is $\mathcal D$. Apply [lem-pur-ringed-site-grothendieck-abelian] to $(\mathcal D,R)$: $\operatorname{Mod}(R)$ is abelian, has all small colimits and exact filtered colimits, and has the displayed generator formed from free sheaves on site objects. The equivalence of step 1 transports these properties and its generator to $\operatorname{Tow}(T,\mathcal O_E)$: universal properties and exactness can be tested after the inverse additive equivalence. Thus the tower category is Grothendieck abelian.

proof.text: Kernels, cokernels and colimits can also be described directly at each level, without identifying the varying-coefficient category with a functor category of modules over one fixed ring. For a tower map $f:M\to N$, put $K_n=\ker(f_n)$ and $Q_n=\operatorname{coker}(f_n)$ in $\operatorname{Mod}(R_n)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-module-sheaves-colimits-forgetful], these have the kernel and cokernel universal properties on underlying abelian sheaves. The equality $f_m t^M_{n,m}=t^N_{n,m}f_n$ induces transitions on $K_n$ and $Q_n$, semilinear because the corresponding transitions on $M,N$ are semilinear; their identities and compositions follow by kernel uniqueness and by cancellation of the cokernel quotient. The componentwise universal maps from or to a test tower commute with transitions by the same uniqueness. Thus these are the kernel and cokernel towers. For a small diagram $(M^i)_i$ of towers, let $L_n=\operatorname{colim}_i M^i_n$ in $\operatorname{Mod}(R_n)$. Its underlying abelian sheaf is the corresponding abelian colimit by the same cited lemma. The maps $M^i_n\to M^i_m\to L_m$ induce an abelian-sheaf map $L_n\to L_m$, which is semilinear: the required equality holds after every colimit injection, and these injections jointly determine a map. The cocycle and the tower-colimit universal property follow by testing after those injections too. In particular filtered colimits are levelwise. Evaluation preserves addition, kernels and cokernels, hence is exact, proving (2) at the abelian level.

proof.text: Use the ordinary localization derived category of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] for the tower category and each $\operatorname{Mod}(R_n)$. Since evaluation is additive and exact by step 3, [lem-sf-exact-functor-derived-triangulated] gives its termwise induced triangulated functor on these unbounded derived categories. This is the functor denoted $C_\bullet\mapsto C_n$ in (2). In particular an evaluation of a quasi-isomorphism of tower complexes is a quasi-isomorphism.

Let $C$ be any complex of towers, viewed as an $R$-module complex on $\mathcal D$. By [lem-pc-kflat-resolution] it admits a quasi-isomorphism $P\to C$ with $P$ K-flat over $R$ and flat in every degree. For each $n$, the underlying sheaf evaluation is the inverse image of the morphism of topoi $e_n$ in [lem-weil-pbc-diagram-site-realization]. We have $e_n^{-1}R=R_n$ by the formula for evaluation in its statement. Give $e_n$ the identity structural ring map to $R_n$. Its module pullback is evaluation: the extra scalar extension is $M_n\otimes_{R_n}R_n\cong M_n$, by $x\otimes a\mapsto ax$ and inverse $x\mapsto x\otimes1$. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-topos-kflat-pullback] applies and shows that every $P_n$ is K-flat over $R_n$ with flat terms. Step 4 shows that $P_n\to C_n$ is a quasi-isomorphism. This supplies simultaneous K-flat models with their strict transitions; it is not deduced from Grothendieck abelianness alone.

proof.text:
Fix $n\geq m\geq1$. On every tower complex $C$ the formula
$$b_{n,m,C}:C_n\otimes_{R_n}R_m\longrightarrow C_m,\qquad x\otimes a\longmapsto a\,t_{n,m}(x)$$
defines a chain map. Indeed $t_{n,m}(r x)=q_{n,m}(r)t_{n,m}(x)$ proves balancing, and the formula commutes with restriction and differentials; by [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product] it therefore induces the asserted map on the sheafified tensor. A tower chain map $f$ commutes with it since $a\,t^D_{n,m}f_n(x)=a\,f_m t^C_{n,m}(x)$. Thus $b$ is natural on complexes and on their homotopy categories. Put $F_{n,m}(C)=C_n\otimes_{R_n}R_m$, valued in $D(R_m)$. This functor on the homotopy category is triangulated: termwise tensor carries a chain homotopy to its tensor, commutes with shift, and carries the cone matrix to the same matrix on the tensored complexes, since it commutes with the two finite summands of a cone. For a quasi-isomorphism $s:P\to P'$ between complexes K-flat with flat terms on $(\mathcal D,R)$, evaluation is a quasi-isomorphism between K-flat complexes by steps 4–5; [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings](1) says $s_n\otimes1$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Together with step 5, these verify the two hypotheses of [lem-pur-left-derived-from-kflat-class] for $F_{n,m}$. Consequently $LF_{n,m}$ exists with its universal comparison $\varepsilon:LF_{n,m}Q\to F_{n,m}$, and $\varepsilon_P$ is invertible on this resolving class.

proof.text:
There is a canonical identification $LF_{n,m}(C)=C_n\otimes^L_{R_n}R_m$. To check it with the universal property just cited, let $H=(-\otimes^L_{R_n}R_m)\circ\operatorname{ev}_n$, where the scalar-extension functor is [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings](2). Its left-derived comparison, applied to $C_n$, gives $HQ\to F_{n,m}$. The universal property of [lem-pur-left-derived-from-kflat-class] gives $H\to LF_{n,m}$. On $P$ from step 5 both comparisons identify their source with $P_n\otimes_{R_n}R_m$, so this map is an isomorphism there. Every derived object is isomorphic to such a $QP$, hence this comparison is an isomorphism everywhere. Now compose $\varepsilon$ with the natural $b$ of step 6 to obtain
$$LF_{n,m}Q\longrightarrow F_{n,m}\longrightarrow\operatorname{ev}_m Q.$$
This transformation descends to $D(\operatorname{Tow})$ using [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]: its two endpoint functors invert quasi-isomorphisms, and its naturality equality for an inverse of a quasi-isomorphism follows by multiplying the equality for that quasi-isomorphism by the two inverse images. It is therefore natural for the arrows of the localization. Under the canonical identification with $H$, the descended map is $\rho_{n,m}:C_n\otimes^L_{R_n}R_m\to C_m$. On a resolving model $P$ it is precisely the formula of step 6. Its construction is natural in $C_\bullet$ and independent of the chosen resolution because it is a transformation between the already defined functors on the localization.

proof.text:
For $r\leq m\leq n$, use one $P$ from step 5. By [lem-pur-kflat-change-of-rings], $P_n\otimes_{R_n}R_m$ is K-flat over $R_m$ with flat terms; [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings] therefore computes the iterated derived scalar extension by the ordinary double tensor. The balancing isomorphism
$$(P_n\otimes_{R_n}R_m)\otimes_{R_m}R_r\xrightarrow{\sim}P_n\otimes_{R_n}R_r,\qquad (x\otimes a)\otimes b\longmapsto x\otimes q_{m,r}(a)b$$
has inverse $x\otimes b\mapsto(x\otimes1)\otimes b$: balancing verifies both composites are identities. These sectionwise balanced maps commute with restrictions and differentials, so [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product] gives the sheaf-complex isomorphism. Along this identification, direct reduction $\rho_{n,r}$ sends $(x\otimes a)\otimes b$ to $q_{m,r}(a)b\,t_{n,r}(x)$. Successive reduction sends it to $b\,t_{m,r}(a\,t_{n,m}(x))=bq_{m,r}(a)t_{m,r}t_{n,m}(x)$, the same element because the strict transitions compose. The formula also commutes with every chain map $P\to P'$; step 7 descends this equality, so it holds for all derived tower objects. For $m=n$ it is the usual unitor $P_n\otimes_{R_n}R_n\to P_n$. For four levels, rebracketing sends $((x\otimes a)\otimes b)\otimes c$ to $x\otimes q_{m,s}(a)q_{r,s}(b)c$ along either parenthesization, so the associativity identifications used in the composition assertion are coherent. This proves the naturality and composition clause of (3).
